title: The Last Mughal: The Fall of Delhi, 1857
author: William Dalrymple
description: A historian's reconstruction of the Delhi rising through Indian and British sources — the letters, trials and personal records of the city's last Mughal court and its people.
context: Dalrymple used the Mutiny Papers held in the National Archives of India — the thousands of documents preserved by the British after the siege — to recover Delhi's Indian voices, previously under-used in the literature.

title: The Azamgarh Proclamation
author: Issued in the name of Feroze Shah (attributed), Azamgarh
description: A proclamation issued at Azamgarh during the rising, calling on Hindus and Muslims to stand together against the East India Company, and addressing landlords, peasants and soldiers.
context: The proclamation is a canonical example of how rebel leaders tried to build unity across religious lines in 1857. It survives because the Company preserved the rebel documents it captured.

title: Queen Victoria's Proclamation
author: Issued in the name of Queen Victoria, Governor-General Canning's government
description: The proclamation announcing the transfer of the Government of India from the East India Company to the British Crown, promising religious toleration and equal admission to state service.
context: Read aloud across India and translated into local languages, the Proclamation ended the Company's rule and set the terms of the new Crown Raj. Historians parse both its promises and its silences.

title: The History of the Indian Mutiny
author: Charles Ball
institution: London: London Printing and Publishing Company
description: One of the earliest full accounts of the 1857 rising, compiled within months of the events and drawing on official reports, newspaper dispatches and correspondence available at the time.
context: Ball wrote as a British author during the events themselves. Useful today as a compendium of how the war looked to its British participants and readers — with all the biases of a wartime source.

title: "The Indian Revolt" — essays for the New-York Daily Tribune
author: Karl Marx
description: A series of articles written for an American newspaper analysing the rebellion as it unfolded, using the dispatches that reached New York.
context: Marx's essays are a fascinating contemporary source: metropolitan, analytic and critical of the Company's rule, while offering interpretations that historians both use and contest. The linked text is the essay "The Revolt in India" of 4 August 1857.

title: Mutiny at the Margins: New Perspectives on the Indian Uprising of 1857
author: Edited by Crispin Bates (with others)
description: A multi-volume academic series charting the lesser-known stories of 1857 — the lives of ordinary soldiers, peasants, artisans and rebels reconstructed from the archives.
context: This is the 'history from below' of 1857 scholarship: it centres subaltern and regional perspectives and re-examines the evidence through a critical lens.

title: Records of the Court-Martial of the 85 Troopers of the 3rd Bengal Light Cavalry
author: East India Company — Bengal Army records
institution: National Archives of India (summary available in secondary literature)
description: The court-martial records of the troopers who refused the greased cartridge at Meerut on 24 April 1857 and were sentenced on 6–8 May — the punishment that helped ignite the garrison.
context: This event is well documented and retold in the secondary literature; the precise shelf reference of the original record should be confirmed against the National Archives of India's finding aids.

title: London Gazette despatch on the storming of Jhansi (Rose's despatch)
author: Major-General Rose's despatch, published by authority
description: The official military despatch reporting the storming of Jhansi on 3 April 1858 — the contemporaneous British account of the assault in which the Rani escaped from the fort.
context: Published in the official gazette weeks after the event, the despatch is the military record of the assault as the command reported it home. It is a partisan but contemporaneous account, to be read alongside Indian traditions of the defence.

title: Histora — Demonstration Document
author: Histora prototype
description: A sample rendering inside Histora's document viewer used to demonstrate the archival-document interface. It is a design artefact, not a historical source.
context: This document exists so visitors can see how the source viewer works without a real scan. It is explicitly labelled as a demonstration and must never be mistaken for an authentic document.

title: Shivaji and His Times
author: Jadunath Sarkar
institution: Initially published 1919; frequently reprinted (e.g., Sangam/Orient reprints)
description: The classic English-language biography of Shivaji, reconstructing his reign from Persian, Marathi and European sources. Modern scholars rely on it while revising several of its judgments.
context: Sarkar's work remains a key reference for the chronology and diplomacy of Shivaji's career, though its treatment of certain episodes (notably the Afzal Khan meeting) is debated.

title: Sabhasad's Bakhar (Shivaji's chronicle — Sabhasad charitra)
author: Krishnaji Anant Sabhasad
institution: Marathi chronicle, written c. 1694–97; English translation by S. N. Sen (1920)
description: A Marathi chronicle of Shivaji's reign written within a generation of his death by a figure close to the court. It is a foundational narrative source for the rise of Swarajya, though its reliability on contested episodes is debated.
context: Bakhars are narrative chronicles with their own literary conventions; they preserve tradition and memory alongside record. Historians use Sabhasad alongside Persian and European documents, cross-checking where the sources diverge. The linked scan is S. N. Sen's 1920 English translation.

title: Shivaji
author: Setumadhavrao Pagdi
description: A concise modern Marathi-and-English biography of Shivaji, useful for the standard chronology and for its balanced treatment of contested events.
context: Pagdi writes within the mainstream of post-Sarkar scholarship, incorporating later archival work on the Maratha period.

title: New History of the Marathas, Vol. I (1600–1707)
author: Govind Sakharam Sardesai
description: The first volume of the standard New History of the Marathas, covering the rise of the Maratha power through Shivaji's era up to 1707.
context: Sardesai's synthesis draws on the extensive Marathi historical sources and remains a standard narrative of the Maratha state's foundation.

title: Contemporaneous accounts of the Afzal Khan affair (Persian and English records)
author: Collected records (Persian chronicles; English factory letters)
description: Persian chronicles and English factory letters that record the death of Afzal Khan at Pratapgad on 10 November 1659 and the ensuing battle. Accounts differ on the details of the meeting.
context: The meeting's circumstances are reconstructed from hostile and friendly testimony alike. Exact references for each surviving account should be verified before citation; the event itself is firmly attested.

title: Records of Shivaji's residence and escape from Agra, 1666 (European factory letters)
author: English, Dutch and other European factory correspondence from Surat and the Deccan

description: Factory letters and intelligence reports that track Shivaji's detention at Agra in 1666 and his escape, corroborating with their own accounts the travails of the visit to court.
context: European correspondents at Surat and in the Deccan followed the affair closely because of trade stakes, and their letters supplement the Marathi and Persian accounts. Shelf references should be verified.

title: Accounts of the Raigad coronation, 1674 (European factory and court records)
author: English, Dutch and Portuguese factory accounts; Marathi chronicles
description: Correspondence and chronicle accounts describing the coronation of 6 June 1674 at Raigad: the ceremonies, the assembly and the new sovereign's titles, including the Chhatrapati proclamation.
context: The coronation is attested from multiple independent directions — foreign factories and Indian chronicles — even though details (who performed what rite, the precise titles) vary between accounts.

title: East India Company factory records — the sack of Surat, January 1664
author: English East India Company records at Surat (letters and diaries)
institution: Published in 'The English Factories in India' (W. Foster, ed.)
description: Surat factory letters and diaries describing the raid of January 1664: the approach of Shivaji's force, the looting of the town and of the English factory itself, and the aftermath in the port.
context: These records are among the most detailed contemporary (if partisan) evidence for the raid, which is also confirmed by Persian chronicles. Exact manuscript references should be verified against the published edition.
